lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Hi Olivia, thanks so much for making the time. Can you hear us okay?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Yep, loud and clear. Sorry, my cat just walked across the keyboard, so if you see a random message in the chat, that was her.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Ha, no worries. She is welcome to apply too, we are hiring.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: So quick intros. I am Priya, I run engineering here at Northwind Labs. This is Arjun, he is a staff engineer on our platform team and he owns most of the ingestion pipeline.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Which means I get paged when it breaks. Which is, you know, less often than last year.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: The plan for today is about forty five minutes. Ten minutes on your background, then Arjun will run a system design exercise, and we will save the last ten minutes for your questions. Sound good?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Sounds great.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Cool. So give us the short version. What have you been working on for the last few years?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Sure. So for the last four years I have been at Relaywave, which is a customer messaging company. I joined as a senior engineer on the data platform team, and for the last two years I have been the tech lead for event ingestion.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: When I joined we were doing maybe forty thousand events a second at peak. When I left we were closer to three hundred thousand, and we had moved off a homegrown queue onto Kafka, with Flink doing most of the enrichment.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Wait, why did you leave? If that is okay to ask.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Totally fair. Honestly, Relaywave got acquired in March, and the platform team is being folded into the parent company's infrastructure org. The work is mostly migration now, and I want to be somewhere smaller where I can shape the product a bit more.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: What was the hardest thing about that Kafka migration? Like the thing that actually kept you up at night.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Ordering guarantees, for sure. We had customers who relied on events arriving in order per user, and the old system gave that to us kind of by accident because it was single threaded per tenant.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: So we had to be really deliberate about partition keys. We ended up keying on tenant plus user, and then we found out three big tenants had these bot users generating like forty percent of their traffic, which made some partitions extremely hot.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Oh, we have that exact problem. How did you handle it?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: We added a salting strategy for known hot keys, with a small registry that the producers read from. It broke strict ordering for those users, but we talked to the customers and it turned out none of them actually cared about ordering for bot traffic.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: I like that you went and asked the customers. That is honestly the answer I was hoping for.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Yeah, it saved us probably two months of engineering. Half the requirements we thought were hard turned out to be assumptions.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Okay, I am going to hand it over to Arjun for the design part.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Great. So this is loosely based on our actual system, so do not be surprised if I get opinionated. We want to design an event ingestion pipeline for a product analytics tool.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Customers send track events from web, mobile and servers. Think about fifty thousand events a second average, with bursts up to five times that. Events need to show up in dashboards within, let us say, sixty seconds, and we need to support replaying data when a customer changes their schema.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Okay. Can I ask a few clarifying questions first?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Please do.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: What is the average event size, and do we need to support backfill from the customer side, like a historical import?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Average is around one kilobyte, though some enterprise customers send ten kilobyte blobs with nested properties. And yes, historical imports are a thing, usually a few hundred million events at once.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: And for the sixty second freshness, is that a p50 or a p99?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Good question. Let us say p95.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Okay. So at the edge, I would put a thin, stateless collector service behind a load balancer. Its only job is auth, basic validation, and writing to a durable log as fast as possible. I would not do any enrichment there.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: It should return a two hundred to the client once the write is acknowledged by the log, so the client SDK can drop the event from its local buffer.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: What happens if the log is slow? Like Kafka is having a bad day.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Then the collectors apply back pressure. The SDKs already retry with jitter, so I would rather return a four twenty nine or a five oh three than buffer in memory on the collector and risk losing data when the pod dies.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Some people say buffer to local disk on the collector.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: You can, and we tried that at Relaywave. It works until a node gets replaced by the autoscaler with forty megabytes of events on its disk. Then you are writing a recovery job at two in the morning.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Yeah, that is, uh, a very specific memory.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Very specific. Anyway. Then from the log, I would split into two paths. A hot path that does enrichment, identity resolution and writes into the columnar store for dashboards, and a cold path that writes raw events to object storage, partitioned by tenant and hour.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: The cold path is basically your source of truth for replays. If a customer changes a schema, you replay from object storage through the same enrichment code, just with a different sink.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: How do you make sure the replay does not starve live traffic?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Separate consumer groups with separate compute, and a rate limit on the replay jobs per tenant. I would also want the columnar store to support writing a new version of a partition and swapping it atomically, so dashboards never show half replayed data.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Okay, we use ClickHouse, so that is roughly partition replace. What about identity resolution? Say an anonymous user logs in and we want to merge their history.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: That one is tricky. I would not rewrite history in the event store. I would keep an identity mapping table, anonymous id to user id, and resolve at query time, with a materialized view for the heavy dashboards. Rewriting billions of rows every time someone logs in just does not scale.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Interesting. We actually do rewrite, in a nightly batch, and it is one of our biggest costs. Maybe thirty percent of our ClickHouse compute.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Oh wow. Yeah, I would look at that. Query time resolution has its own costs, the joins get expensive, but you can cache the mapping pretty aggressively.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Arjun, write that down, that might be the most valuable thing we get out of this hour.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Already did. Okay, last piece. How do you think about multi tenancy? One of our Enterprise customers is doing about a third of our total volume.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: I would start with shared infrastructure and noisy neighbor protection. Per tenant quotas at the collector, and weighted fair queuing in the consumers. Then once a tenant crosses some threshold, maybe ten percent of volume, you give them dedicated partitions and possibly a dedicated consumer pool.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: The important thing is that the code path is the same. Dedicated should be a config change, not a fork of the pipeline.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: And how would you monitor freshness? Like how do you know you are hitting that sixty second target?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: I would inject synthetic canary events per region every ten seconds and measure end to end time until they are queryable. Consumer lag is useful, but it does not tell you whether the dashboards are actually fresh.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Nice. Okay, I think I have what I need. Priya, anything you want to dig into?

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: One question. Staff engineers here spend maybe half their time not writing code. Tell me about a time you had to influence a decision you did not own.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Sure. Last year our product team wanted to launch real time alerts, and they had promised a big customer a ten second latency. The pipeline could not do that without roughly doubling our infrastructure spend.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: I did not own the roadmap, so instead of just saying no, I wrote a two page doc with three options and the cost of each. Ten seconds was about ninety thousand dollars a year extra, thirty seconds was basically free.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: We went back to the customer with thirty seconds and they were totally fine with it. The product lead actually started inviting me to planning after that.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: That is great. And was there a time it did not go your way?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Oh, definitely. I pushed hard for us to adopt a schema registry, and I lost that argument twice. In hindsight I was pitching it as a technical nicety rather than connecting it to the incidents it would have prevented. The third time I brought the incident list, and it got approved.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Ha, third time is the charm. Okay, we have about ten minutes. What questions do you have for us?

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: A few. First, how big is the engineering team, and how is it structured?

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: We are eleven engineers, plus a small ML group. Three product pods, a platform team of four, which Arjun is on, and Hannah's ML folks working on our AI Insights feature. This role would sit on platform, but with a lot of cross team scope.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: And what is the biggest technical problem you want this person to solve in the first six months?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Honestly, reliability and cost of ingestion. We had two freshness incidents last quarter where dashboards were more than fifteen minutes behind, and the nightly identity rewrite we just talked about. Those are the two big ones.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: And there is a bigger bet coming. AI Insights needs a lot of the same data, with different access patterns, and we need someone to make sure we do not build a second pipeline by accident.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Got it. What does on call look like?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: One week in six for platform, with a follow the sun handoff to our contractor in Lisbon overnight. We average maybe two pages a week, and we do a blameless review for anything customer facing.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: That is reasonable. Last question. How do you think about remote? The posting said hybrid.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: We have an office in Austin, and people come in Tuesday and Wednesday if they are local. But about half the team is fully remote, and we fly everyone in once a quarter for planning. You would be fine remote.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Great. That answers everything for now.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Awesome. So next steps. We will get back to you by Friday. If it goes well, the next round is a conversation with Dana, our CEO, and a pairing session with one of the product teams.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Perfect. Thanks, both of you. This was genuinely fun, I do not usually get to argue about identity resolution in an interview.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Ha, anytime. I might email you about it anyway.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Thanks Olivia. Talk soon.

lines.speaker: olivia
lines.text: Bye!

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Okay, she dropped. Arjun, quick gut check before we write up the scorecards?

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Strong yes from me. The system design was really solid, and the identity resolution idea alone could save us real money. The only gap is she has not worked much with ClickHouse specifically.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: I do not think that matters, she clearly understands columnar stores. I am also a strong yes. The influence story was exactly what we need.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Agreed. I will get my scorecard into Greenhouse by end of day today.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Great. I will set up the loop with Dana for early next week and ping the recruiter to move fast, I suspect she has other offers.

lines.speaker: arjun
lines.text: Sounds good. Nice one.
